World of Warcraft Forums

# UI Add-On Development Policy

Guides UI and Macro

[Kaivax](https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Kaivax) (Kaivax) November 19, 2018, 9:09pm 1

7/15/2009 Music Distribution through UI Add-Ons

##  We have recently seen a number of User Interface Add-Ons that are making modifications to the World of Warcraft in-game music files and wanted to take a moment to go over some important points with the community in connection with this. While we are currently allowing Add-Ons that remove or replace existing sound files, keep in mind that it is illegal to distribute copyrighted materials, in this case in-game music and audio files, without authorization. One of the primary goals of the user interface is to allow players to customize their game experience and we hope to avoid making any modifications in the future that will prevent this.

4/13/2009 UI Add-On Development Policy Update
On March 20, we released the new add-on development policy to the public as an ongoing effort to help ensure add-on integrity, safety, and quality for the community. Since that time we have been in touch with many UI development communities on what the policy means to them and the continuing development of these add-ons. We would like to announce further that we are providing a sixty-day grace period beginning at the time of the initial release of the policy for UI developers to comply with the new policy. After May 19th, Blizzard Entertainment will begin to enforce the Add-on Development policy, and developers found to be in violation of this policy will be contacted directly.

* * *

World of Warcraft User Interface Add-On Development Policy

With the continuing popularity of World of Warcraft user interface add-ons (referred to hereafter as “add-ons”) created by the community of players, Blizzard Entertainment has formalized design and distribution guidelines for add-ons.
These guidelines have been put in place to ensure the integrity of World of Warcraft and to help promote an enjoyable gaming environment for all of our players - failure to abide by them may result in measures up to and including taking formal legal action.

1) Add-ons must be free of charge.  
All add-ons must be distributed free of charge. Developers may not create “premium” versions of add-ons with additional for-pay features, charge money to download an add-on, charge for services related to the add-on, or otherwise require some form of monetary compensation to download or access an add-on.

2) Add-on code must be completely visible.  
The programming code of an add-on must in no way be hidden or obfuscated, and must be freely accessible to and viewable by the general public.

3) Add-ons must not negatively impact World of Warcraft realms or other players.
Add-ons will perform no function which, in Blizzard Entertainment’s sole discretion, negatively impacts the performance of the World of Warcraft realms or otherwise negatively affects the game for other players. For example, this includes but is not limited to excessive use of the chat system, unnecessary loading from the hard disk, and slow frame rates.

4) Add-ons may not include advertisements.  
Add-ons may not be used to advertise any goods or services.

5) Add-ons may not solicit donations.  
Add-ons may not include requests for donations. We recognize the immense amount of effort and resources that go into developing an add-on; however, such requests should be limited to the add-on website or distribution site and should not appear in the game.

6) Add-ons must not contain offensive or objectionable material.  
World of Warcraft has been given a “T” by the ESRB, and similar ratings from other ratings boards around the world.
Blizzard Entertainment requires that add-ons not include any material that would not be allowed under these ratings.

7) Add-ons must abide by World of Warcraft ToU and EULA.  
All add-ons must follow the World of Warcraft Terms of Use and the World of Warcraft End User License Agreement.

8) Blizzard Entertainment has the right to disable add-on functionality as it sees fit.  
To maintain the integrity World of Warcraft and ensure the best possible gaming experience for our players, Blizzard Entertainment reserves the right to disable any add-on functionality within World of Warcraft at its sole discretion. For more information…

If you are an add-on developer and have any questions about and this User Interface Add-On Development Policy and how it pertains to the add-on that you’ve developed, please don’t hesitate to email us at WoWUI@blizzard.com .

# Paywalled & ‘Premium’ Addons Violate Blizzard Policy

I wanted to share some of the policy language for future reference and hopefully get some eyes on this.

It's not explicitly spelled out in the high-level Blizzard EULA, it is defined in Blizzard's UI Add-On Development Policy and Developer/API Terms, which are incorporated into the Terms of Service we all agree to when using Blizzard Games.

The Blizzard UI Add-On Development Policy:

> _“All add-ons must be distributed free of charge. Developers may not create ‘premium’ versions of add-ons with additional for-pay features, charge money to download an add-on, charge for services related to the add-on, or otherwise require some form of monetary compensation to download or access an add-on.”_
> 
> 

Key points of interest:

* Charging to download an addon.
* Locking features behind payment.
* "Premium" or paid tiers of the same addon.
* Requiring payment to access or use addon functionality.

**So why are Content Creators doing this currently with all these "Ui" packages?**

Additionally, Blizzard states in the Developers / API Terms of Use similar restrictions for any application or addon that uses Blizzards APIs:

> _“Applications may not charge premiums to use the APIs. ‘Premium’ versions offering additional for-pay features are not permitted, nor can users be charged money to download or access an application or its services.”_
> 
> 

The more important part that seems to have gotten away from Content Creators.

Donations are allowed:

* Must be completely optional. (If you enjoy something, support a dev!)
* Not tied to features, access, performance, or updates.
* Not required to unlock or enable any part of the addon.

_**TLDR; Addons must be fully functional and accessible for free.
Paywalling, premium features, or monetized access violates Blizzard policy.**_

A unofficial list of addons that require a "Paid or Premium"

* Content Creator UI addon packages
* TSM Premium
* Zygor Guides (Base is free, paying for the guide)
* RestedXP
* Paid WeakAura Packs / Custom strings (ambiguous)
* Archon Addon

Links for reference:

<https://us.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/t/ui-add-on-development-policy/24534>

<https://www.blizzard.com/en-us/legal/fba4d00f-c7e4-4883-b8b9-1b4500a402ea/blizzard-end-user-license-agreement>

World of Warcraft Forums

# Addons behind a paywall? Do Blizzard not adhere to their own ToS?

Community General Discussion

[Candi-1510586](https://eu.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Candi-1510586) (Candi) March 17, 2026, 2:04pm 1

I’ve been reading Blizzard’s addon policy, and two parts stand out to me:

* **1) Add-ons must be free of charge.**  
  All add-ons must be distributed free of charge. Developers may not create “premium” versions with additional paid features or require monetary compensation to access an add-on.
* **2) Add-on code must be completely visible.**  
  The code must not be hidden or obfuscated and should be freely accessible to the public.

Given that, I’m struggling to understand how some popular addons (like RestedXP, Zygor, Progresstools, etc.) fit within these rules.

From what I can see:

* Some features—if not most—such as guides or updates, are locked behind payment (Patreon, Twitch subs, etc.)

...

But a lot of actual players at time can seem like bots, so not so easy to identify.

Hopefully, someone using a banned add-on will be easier to detect.

The other way of course is to see what these add-ons do and see if they can add functions to the game to mitigate some of the benefits of those add-ons.

Of course players would need to be a bit more understanding of what they’re trying to achieve.

[Jito-536](https://eu.forums.blizzard.com/en/wow/u/Jito-536) (Jito) March 17, 2026, 11:20pm 20

It’s easier for Blizzard to ban bots, because it’s very clear in the ToS that those are not allowed, and any players that buy and use a botting program are guilty of breaking the ToS.

But addons are different. For one, then it’s difficult to police the whole pay-driven sub-market of addons, and secondly, then it’s difficult for both addon creators and players to know what addons are okay and which ones might be ostracized by Blizzard.

[mystery](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/mystery) March 20, 2009, 3:59pm 1

Blizzard just released a new [UI Addon Development policy](http://www.worldofwarcraft.com/policy/ui.html) , which details, among other things:

> 1. Add-ons must be free of charge.  
>    All add-ons must be distributed free of charge. Developers may not create “premium” versions of add-ons with additional for-pay features, charge money to download an add-on, charge for services related to the add-on, or otherwise require some form of monetary compensation to download or access an add-on.

> 

I guess I shouldn’t have paid for a full version of Carbonite, then.

[RobotPants](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/RobotPants) March 20, 2009, 4:04pm 2

Are there really that many that charge? It seems pretty silly to not even allow people to take donations.

[mouselock](https://forum.quartertothree.

...

com/u/Lorini) March 20, 2009, 5:15pm 7

I don’t see how they can enforce it, except through trademark. The add-ons don’t use Blizzard code, only the macro language.

I don’t agree with it at all, and I neither develop for nor pay for any Blizzard add-ons. What they are now forcing people to do is to make their own product better for free.

[Derek\_French](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/Derek_French) March 20, 2009, 5:19pm 8

Wow, really, there were mods that cost? That’s crazy. I can’t believe it was ever allowed in the first place.

And yeah, website requests for donations are fine. I have donated for software before.

[Athryn](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/Athryn) March 20, 2009, 5:23pm 9

I am with Lorini, I think this is a poor move on Blizzard’s part.

...

Much like the way people can’t sell accounts or gold.

[Lorini](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/Lorini) March 20, 2009, 7:52pm 14

But it’s actually very different. Accounts are owned by Blizzard, that’s obvious. The gold is also owned by Blizzard. The code however you create yourself. That’s the difference that I see.

The other thing is that AH prices are numbers, they aren’t a copy of something in the game.

[Kael](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/Kael) March 20, 2009, 9:03pm 15

Overall I think this is an attempt by Blizzard to, if not kill, then damage the modding community. They want to deflate the value of modding by taking away the incentives. Im guessing because they think that cheating through UI mods is to prevelant and their is to many good reasons to do it.

1) Add-ons must be free of charge.

I think this is just because of point number 2. If you allowed mods to charge and forced them all to show their code, then no one would pay anyway.
Someone would just copy the code and release their own version for half the price (or for free) and it would kill the developer anyway.

2) Add-on code must be completely visible.

This is the most obvious anti-cheating method. If WoW suspects a mod may cheat they want to be able to check it out. If they find evidence that it does in the code, or the code isnt available or doesnt match what the UI has been doing they banish the players and disable players using the mod.

3) Add-ons must not negatively impact World of Warcraft realms or other players.

This one is obvious, Im all for it.

4) Add-ons may not include advertisements.

This is a block to keep developers from getting money through their efforts. Still why would WoW care if a player opted to see advertisements as he played?

5) Add-ons may not solicit donations.

As before they are shutting down ways to make money.

6) Add-ons must not contain offensive or objectionable material.
Again if I want an addon that causes my dwarf to cuss whenever he takes damage why does WoW care? Modding has never been bound by the rating (otherwise Fall from Heaven would be in some trouble).

7) Add-ons must abide by World of Warcraft ToU and EULA.

As in 6, why should my modifications of my game be forced to comply with the games rating? If I want to draw a penis on spiderman in my comic books or if I want to edit my cd sounds and insert cuss words why should that be illegal?

I can understand that they shouldn’t effect other players. But whats the harm in effectign the player himself?

8) Blizzard Entertainment has the right to disable add-on functionality as it sees fit.

This Im perfectly fine with this.

[Daagar](https://forum.quartertothree.com/u/Daagar) March 20, 2009, 9:22pm 16

I see this as partially for a way for Blizzard to not be held liable for someone purchasing CrapModA and then hounding blizzard because they got ripped off/it doesn’t work/whatever.
